title: Buffalo Soldiers
full_review:
A sly American GI running scams on a U.S. Army base in West Germany near the close of the Cold War gets a taste of his own medicine in the pitch-black satire, "Buffalo Soldiers" (Miramax).

In this film adapted from Robert O'Connor's 1993 novel, director Gregor Jordan misfires with a skewed attack on military honor, lacing the film with a toxic cynicism that undercuts its otherwise darkly humorous satirizing of American free enterprise.
At the center of the action is Ray Elwood (Joaquin Phoenix), a brash Army supply clerk and consummate con man. Having been given two options -- enlist or go to prison -- Elwood, like many of his fellow former delinquent barracks buddies, is merely serving time. With Cold War tensions thawing, they are left with little to fight except boredom.

Using his access, Elwood operates a lucrative business reselling overstocked cleaning supplies on the off-base black market and cooking up batches of heroin in an abandoned hangar, all under the nose of Col. Wallace Berman (Ed Harris) -- the most incompetent brass buffoon since Capt. Parmenter on "F Troop." When not being played the fool by Elwood's ingratiating charm, Berman is henpecked by his verbally castrating wife (Elizabeth McGovern), an aging vixen who's entertained more troops than Bob Hope.

In the confusion caused by a runaway tank, manned by two stoned slackers, Elwood stumbles across a truckload of army munitions. Rather than return them, Elwood decides to unload the windfall on a Turkish arms dealer willing to pay top dollar for the weapons. However, Elwood's bulletproof luck changes when a new officer, Sgt. Robert Lee (Scott Glenn), an old-school, brush-cut Vietnam vet intent on cleaning house, begins to breathe down his neck, immediately targeting Elwood for some Army-style discipline.
Proving that two can play the game, Elwood starts dating Lee's daughter, Robyn (Anna Paquin), a move that only serves to ratchet up the graying warrior's determination to break Elwood. As the Berlin Wall is set to crumble, Elwood finds himself fending off Lee's frontal assault, while flanked by Turkish terrorists and targeted by friendly fire, as members of his own base turn up the heat for their cut of the action.

While Phoenix, to his credit, injects his performance with sufficient buoyant energy to make an otherwise repellent character engaging enough to watch, his portrayal of the happy-go-lucky hustler does little to remedy the near-systemic pessimism that fuels much of the narrative.

Challenging the myth of the soldier's "code of honor" is not novel to the cinema; it's been done effectively countless times in both dramas and comedies. But rather than merely questioning this perhaps over-romanticized notion, Gregor seems hell-bent on demolishing any possibility of belief in virtue among members of the armed forces, neatly dividing his characters into three stereotyped ranks -- careerists, clowns or cons. It is the amoral Elwood who is the hero, not because he is virtuous, but because he, unlike the officers -- and by inference the entire military and economic machine that they serve -- doesn't hide behind the pretension of virtue.

Unlike Robert Altman's groundbreaking 1970 "MASH," which used the lance of comedy to lightly lampoon long-established beliefs about the military, the crude mocking tone of "Buffalo Soldiers" undermines many of the weighty issues raised by the film concerning the hypocrisy of war and the dark side of capitalism unfettered by morality.

More disturbing is the movie's wink-wink ending which seems to misguidedly suggest that crime -- or at least bending the rules for one's advantage -- not only pays, but is rewarded. This win-at-all-costs attitude is characterized by the telling tagline chosen by the filmmakers: "Steal all you can steal," a contemptuously sardonic spin on the Army's recruitment pitch: "Be all that you can be."

As a film, "Buffalo Soldiers" aptly resembles the horned animal of its title: a point here, a point there and a lot of bull in between.

Due to a benign attitude toward felony, some sexual situations, recurring violence and drug abuse, as well as much rough language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
